23:1-3 The Savior Proclaims: "Great Are the Words of Isaiah"

quotes.text: On numerous occasions the Lord has commanded his disciples to search the scriptures in order to learn and live the doctrines of salvation. During his mortal ministry, the Savior stated, "Search the scriptures; … they are they which testify of me" (John 5:39). During his appearance on the Western Hemisphere following his resurrection, Christ quoted from the scriptures and then said to the Nephites: "Ye ought to search these things. Yea, a commandment I give unto you that ye search these things diligently" (3 Nephi 23:1). In our day the Lord enjoins his followers to "search these commandments, for they are true and faithful, and … shall all be fulfilled" (D&C 1:37).
quotes.speaker: Merrill J. Bateman

quotes.text: Ye ought to search these things] The Savior has just quoted Isaiah 54 so he is commanding us to search the writings of Isaiah. Elder Bruce R. Mc Conkie wrote: "If our eternal salvation depends upon our ability to understand the writings of Isaiah as fully and truly as Nephi understood them-and who shall say that such is not the case!-how shall we fare in that great day when with Nephi we shall stand before the pleasing bar of Him who said: 'Great are the words of Isaiah'? ... "It just may be that my salvation (and yours also!) does in fact depend upon our ability to understand the writings of Isaiah as fully and truly as Nephi understood them. For that matter, why should either Nephi or Isaiah know anything that is withheld front us? Does not that God who is no respecter of persons treat all his children alike? Has he not Oven us his promise and recited to us the terms and conditions of his law pursuant to which he will reveal to us what he has revealed to them?" ("Ten Keys to Understanding Isaiah," Ensign, October 1973, p. 78)

It is quite another for the Lord to quote someone and then to command the Saints to search that prophet's writings! what greater recommendation could there be for us to begin a life-long search and study of Isaiah?

Two aspects of the text in the record of Samuel's prophecy shed further convincing evidence on the question. First of all, as noted above, the statement of the resurrection of the saints is out of chronological order in the reiteration of the events signifying the death of the Savior. It is placed in the midst of the description of the natural violence of that time, rather than after the darkness lifted, which is when it would have occurred. Indeed, Mc Conkie and Millet point out the problem by noting "The rise of many Saints from the graves was not, strictly speaking, a sign of his death, but rather took place at the time of the Lord's resurrection." [15] As previously noted, placing verse 25 after verse 27 would restore the proper order and remove this inconsistency. The second and a most compelling argument lies in the literary structure of verses 2027. While not all the recorded words of Samuel from the city wall may be in chiastic form, substantial portions are. An excerpt is shown in the Appendix. Even a cursory examination reveals that most of this is strongly chiastic, with obvious parallelisms at several levels and no out-of-place elements. In fact, the chiastic forms found so profusely throughout all books of scripture rarely, if ever, show such a blatant break in symmetry and order as is in the passage in question, particularly where it could have been "fixed" so easily, as we see here (by moving verse 25 to immediately follow verse 27). The present author has discovered several hundred chiasms and lesser numbers of other parallel forms in all four of the Standard Works.[16][17][18][19][20] It is extremely rare to find an element out of order, and none other that he has observed could be corrected as easily as this one. Thus it may be concluded that the broken symmetry in these verses is not the product of the original author of the passage, but is the result of a later insertion, at the behest of the Savior, as described above. Assuming this to be so, we gain insight into the writing, abridging and translation of the Book of Mormon from these passages. Among other things, we know that Samuel did not write the record, for he jumped from the wall, fled, and was never seen again among the Nephites.[21] Moreover, he would not have omitted the prophecy. Whether the passage was spoken in chiastic form or not, whoever wrote the account took great pains to write it so, but forgetting the one prophecy. The younger Nephi did not rewrite the account, but simply wrote in the margin or between the lines. He probably was constrained by the availability of space on the plate in the placement of the missing scripture. Even if he understood the literary structure of the passage, he may not have been able to find room to preserve it in the insertion of the missing scripture. Perhaps the most important consequence of this finding is the understanding it provides of how Mormon abridged the records in writing the Book of Mormon. Here he obviously copied the corrected account verbatim into his abridgment for, if he had paraphrased or otherwise written the text himself, he could have balanced the passage quite simply as shown above. Of course, there are other evidences that this was his practice, including wordprint analysis.[22] Finally, it is clear that Joseph Smith followed the original language very closely in his translation, preserving the modified structure. It may be wondered to what extent the original authors of the Book of Mormon, and the compiler, Mormon, were conscious of the chiastic structure that occurs so commonly in that book. More significantly, it is quite likely that the young and unschooled Joseph Smith was completely unaware of the form as he was translating the record. Chiasmus had hardly been noticed by the scholars of the day,[23] and the first detailed discussion of the subject was not published until ten years after his death. [24] The presence of extensive chiasmus helps refute the claim by some that the Book of Mormon is the product of a nineteenth century author, as has already been discussed well. [25] First of all, modern writers hardly use chiasmus at all. Moreover, if a modern writer had stumbled upon chiasmus and used it in writing the book, he would not have written a passage as flawed, and as easily corrected, as the one under consideration. Before going on, it would be well to examine certain aspects of the text more closely. The recorded words of the Savior in 23:11 might be interpreted as indicating that the fulfillment of the prophecy, rather than the prophecy itself, had not been recorded, and several have so stated, including Sperry [7] and Mc Conkie, Millett and Top [8]. On the other hand, others have said that the prophecy was missing, including Ludlow [9] and the authors of the Book of Mormon Student Manual published by the Church [10]. Each of these authors has simply stated his opinion matter-of-factly, without discussion or justification. In addition to these, the heading of Chapter 23 for the last several editions of the Book of Mormon states "The words of Samuel the Lamanite concerning the resurrection are added to their records". There is no record in the Book of Mormon of the fulfillment of the prophecy. Of course, perhaps Mormon would have found it unnecessary to mention the fulfillment, given the present dialogue. Since he selected his material to maximize its impact on future generations,[11] what did he gain by bringing the subject up in the present context? Certainly the Savior's concern for completeness and accuracy in the scriptures is taught effectively. This is reinforced immediately afterward when the Savior recites Malachi's writings. Might there be another, more subtle, reason? Could he be teaching us something about the manner of the writing, abridgment, and translation of the Book of Mormon? Consider the following. There are several indications that it was the prophecy that was missing. The Savior's question in verse 9 appears to support this interpretation. If the prophecy had been written in the records he had before him, it is doubtful that he would have reminded them of it. More than likely he would simply have reminded them that they hadn't recorded the fulfillment. Their response, "Yea, Lord, Samuel did prophesy according to thy words...", is consistent with a missing record of the prophecy. Such a statement would not have been called for if they were looking at the written prophecy. There is also the question of timing. Although some have concluded that the Savior's visit came several months after the crucifixion,[12] there are good indications that his visit was immediately after His resurrection. Verse 18 of chapter 10 says that "in the ending of the thirty and fourth year" the people had "great favors shown unto them, and great blessings poured out upon their heads". It also says that "soon after the ascension of Christ into heaven he did truly manifest himself unto them--showing his body unto them...". We read later that he visited with them three days, and than afterward came many times over what could be presumed to be several months.[13] Perhaps the great blessings spoken of as being received at the end of the year were at the culmination of his many visits, rather than at the beginning. The first two verses of chapter 11 strongly imply that the visit was within a day or so of the resurrection. People would hardly be expected to still be "marveling and wondering, and... showing one another the great and marvelous change which had taken place" nearly a year after the event. Would they have had time, a day or two after the three days of darkness and the great disruption of their homes, lives and everything else, to record anything at all? It might be argued that forty years is a long time to remember an unrecorded prophecy, particularly with a change in church leadership (Nephi turned the records over to his son Nephi, and left Zarahemla, about 1 BC[14]). But the younger Nephi would have been well acquainted with the dramatic confrontation between the rebellious Nephites and Samuel, if not actually present, it having taken place just four years before he received the records, and can be expected to have remembered this event, as well as Samuel's prophecies, for the rest of his life. quotes.text: Therefore, give heed unto the teachings of those we have sent among you, and let all strife, animosity, and contention cease in your midst; live your religion, and let peace, faith, charity, and good works abound.

The resurrected Jesus made a special point of ensuring that this glorious event—witnessed alike on two hemispheres, and in which all mortals have an inexpressibly important and personal stake—was likewise carefully recorded. In fact, Jesus, noting the neglect of Samuel's prophecy, commanded that it be written. (See 3 Nephi 23:9-11.) No wonder, for He anticipated the subsequent reactions to the reality of the resurrection, such as those of the Athenians to Paul's preaching: ‘And when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked: and others said, We will hear thee again of this matter.’ (Acts 17:32.) “Jesus, the Jehovah of the Old Testament (who had been so careful to see that much lesser facts were carefully established in the mouths of two or three witnesses), insisted that the two central facts of human history, the atonement and the resurrection, be carefully established in the pages of the two great written witnesses of Him and the resurrection. “Such careful correlation and amplified attesting would surely not surprise previous prophets—nor should it us. “The above is not recited just to note how reassuringly tidy the restored gospel is, nor how impressively exacting about facts the Lord is. Instead, one should ask, ‘What knowledge does the world need to have more than the sure testimony and evidence that Jesus is the Christ and that His atonement actually accomplished God's great plan of redemption, whereby mankind will be blessed with immortality?’ In a world filled increasingly with drift, disbelief, and despair, what more welcome ‘good news’ could be given?
